title: Relational Algebra
html:
Relational algebra is a mathematical procedural query language containing operations to retrieve data. Relational calculus is its non-procedural, declarative counterpart.

Relational Algebra Operators

Selection (σ)

Filters rows based on a logical predicate. Removes no columns.

Projection (π)

Selects specified columns and discards others. Removes duplicates automatically in relational theory.

Union (∪)

Combines rows from two tables. Both tables must be union-compatible (same number of columns, matching domain types in order).

Set Difference (-)

Returns rows present in the first table but not in the second table. Must be union-compatible.

Cartesian Product (×)

Combines every row of the left table with every row of the right table. Output columns = Sum of columns; Output rows = Product of rows.

Natural Join (⋈)

Joins tables based on matching column names and data types, removing duplicate join columns from the output.

Theta Join (⋈θ)

An inner join that combines rows using an arbitrary comparison condition θ (e.g. =, <, >, ≤, ≥, ≠).

Division (÷)

Used for queries containing the word "all". R ÷ S returns tuples in R that are paired with every tuple in S.

Relational Calculus Syntax Comparison

Aspect Tuple Relational Calculus (TRC) Domain Relational Calculus (DRC)
Variables Variables represent entire rows (tuples). e.g., t Variables represent individual attributes (domains). e.g., x, y, z
Query focus Filters rows. Very close to SQL concept. Filters values in columns directly. More abstract.
Syntax { t | P(t) } { <x1, x2, ...> | P(x1, x2, ...) }
Example Query
(Get Names of Students in CS dept)		 { t.Name | t ∈ Students ∧ t.Dept = 'CS' } { <n> | ∃ i, d (<i, n, d> ∈ Students ∧ d = 'CS') }
